name: Few-Shot Examples
question: Will examples help, or will the model copy them?
summary: A few input–output examples in the prompt show the model the format, tone and decisions you want, often better than description alone. But models pick up whatever the examples share: the most common label, the last label, the length, even irrelevant surface features. Use a handful of diverse, balanced examples that cover edge cases, vary their order, and consider retrieving the most similar examples for each input.
useCases: Classification and extraction with subtle categories
A house style or format that is easier to show than describe
Edge cases the instructions alone keep getting wrong

steps.title: Collect real, labelled examples
steps.text: Examples come from real tickets with checked labels, including awkward ones. Invented examples tend to be too clean.

steps.title: Balance the labels
steps.text: One example per label means no label dominates. Four refunds out of five had pushed predicted refunds to 60%.

steps.title: Pick the most similar
steps.text: For each label, the example closest to this complaint is chosen, so the demonstrations are relevant to the case at hand.

steps.title: Shuffle the order
steps.text: The last example’s label gets copied more often. Shuffling removes a fixed recency bias.

steps.title: Wrap examples in tags
steps.text: Tags separate examples from instructions and from the real complaint, so the model does not confuse them.

steps.title: Measure per label
steps.text: Average accuracy can hide bias. Compare the share of each predicted label with the true share; a big gap means the model is copying the examples.

practice.scenario: An e-commerce company classifies complaints into refund, delivery, damage and billing. Its prompt had five examples, four of them refunds, and the model labelled 60% of complaints as refunds when the true share was 30%. Replacing them with balanced examples retrieved by similarity for each complaint raised accuracy to 91%.

samples.code:
import random
import numpy as np

EXAMPLES = load_labelled_examples()        # [{"text": ..., "label": ..., "vec": np.array}]
LABELS = ["refund", "delivery", "damage", "billing"]

def pick_examples(query_vec, per_label=1):
    """Most similar example for each label: balanced and relevant."""
    chosen = []
    for label in LABELS:
        pool = [e for e in EXAMPLES if e["label"] == label]
        best = max(pool, key=lambda e: float(np.dot(e["vec"], query_vec)))
        chosen.extend([best][:per_label])
    random.shuffle(chosen)                  # no fixed order, no recency bias
    return chosen

def build_prompt(complaint: str, query_vec) -> str:
    shots = "\n".join(f"<example><text>{e['text']}</text><label>{e['label']}</label></example>"
                      for e in pick_examples(query_vec))
    return (f"Classify the complaint as one of: {', '.join(LABELS)}.\n"
            f"<examples>\n{shots}\n</examples>\n<complaint>{complaint}</complaint>")

numericDrill.question: True complaint labels are 30% refund, 30% delivery, 20% damage and 20% billing. With skewed examples the model predicts refund for 60% of complaints. If every true refund is still labelled refund, what share of all complaints is wrongly labelled refund, in percent?
numericDrill.answer: 60% predicted refund minus 30% that really are refunds leaves 30% of all complaints wrongly labelled refund. Those errors come from the other labels, so accuracy can fall by up to 30 points.

interview.question: Why can few-shot examples make a model worse?
interview.answer: Models pick up patterns the examples share, including ones you did not intend: the most common label, the label of the last example, their length or their wording. Skewed or unrepresentative examples bias outputs towards them. Balanced, diverse examples in varied order avoid this.

interview.question: When should you retrieve examples dynamically?
interview.answer: When the input space is broad and a fixed handful cannot cover it, or when the best example depends on the input. Retrieving the most similar labelled examples for each input, balanced across labels, gives relevant demonstrations without paying for dozens of static ones on every call.
